title: India Has Waived Customs Duty on Nuclear Equipment Going Back Seven Years. The Market Noticed.
excerpt: The retrospective exemption formalises an unwritten practice, cuts project costs, and sends nuclear stocks surging as India chases 100 GW by 2047.
body:
India's finance ministry has waived customs duties on all equipment imported for nuclear power generation over the past seven years — formalising what was already an unwritten industry practice and sending nuclear stocks surging.

The notification, issued on June 11 under Section 28A of the Customs Act, covers imports of non-irradiated fuel elements, cartridges, and reactor equipment classified under tariff item 8401 30 00, made between April 1, 2019, and January 31, 2026. Importers will not face any retrospective duty demands for shipments during that period.

The government acknowledged that customs duty had not been levied on these goods as a matter of practice for years, but the position had never been formally codified. The latest order does exactly that — regularising the past and removing any lingering tax liability.

## Building on Budget 2026

The retrospective waiver follows the Union Budget released in February, which extended the customs duty exemption for nuclear power equipment all the way to 2035. An earlier notification in October 2025 had granted the exemption on a prospective basis. The June 11 order closes the gap by reaching back to 2019.

The policy is expected to lower project costs and reduce the unit cost of electricity generated from nuclear plants, making them more commercially viable. It also clears the path for faster customs clearances, which had been a persistent bottleneck in equipment deliveries to nuclear construction sites.

## India's 100 GW Nuclear Ambition

The duty waiver is part of a broader push to scale India's nuclear capacity from its current base of roughly 8 GW to 100 GW by 2047 — a target that the Department of Atomic Energy has called essential for India's net-zero commitment by 2070.

The SHANTI Act of 2025 opened the nuclear sector to greater private participation for the first time, and the duty exemption makes that entry more attractive. Critical equipment covered under the waiver includes reactor pressure vessels, steam generators, pressurizers, and turbines for the light-water reactors being built with foreign cooperation — components that India cannot yet manufacture domestically at scale.

The primary beneficiary is the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL), the state-run operator that imports fuel assemblies for the country's reactor fleet. But the ripple effects extend to the entire nuclear supply chain.

## Markets Respond

Nuclear-linked stocks rallied after the notification. MTAR Technologies, which manufactures precision-engineered components for India's fast breeder reactor programme, surged 13 per cent. The company has supplied roughly 70 per cent of the components for India's prototype fast breeder reactor, with each reactor representing a revenue opportunity of nearly ₹1,500 crore.

Walchandnagar Industries, which makes Class-I equipment for nuclear reactors, rose around 6 per cent. Power Mech Projects, which recently entered the nuclear infrastructure segment with a ₹563-crore contract from BHEL, gained a similar amount.

At the end of FY26, the civilian nuclear segment accounted for 26.3 per cent of MTAR's ₹2,582-crore order book — a share that analysts expect to grow as more reactors move from planning to construction.

## The Diaspora Investment Case

For NRIs watching India's energy transition, the nuclear sector is increasingly difficult to ignore. The combination of duty-free imports, private-sector entry under the SHANTI Act, and a 100 GW target by 2047 creates a multi-decade infrastructure opportunity that is still in its early stages.

India currently operates 24 nuclear reactors and has 8 more under construction. But the gap between 8 GW and 100 GW is enormous — and closing it will require tens of billions of dollars in equipment, fuel, and construction, much of it imported. The duty waiver ensures that at least one cost barrier has been permanently removed.
